question: A team lead is explaining hallucinations to colleagues who are new to using Claude at work. Which two statements should she include because they are accurate? Select two.
options: A) They occur mainly in long responses, so keeping answers short avoids the problem well.
B) They only occur when Claude has no access to the web and must rely on what it knows.
C) They can appear in answers that read fluently and hold together from start to finish.
D) They are a known limit of current frontier models, not a sign of a broken setup.
E) They can be removed entirely by instructing Claude to answer only when it is certain.
correct_answers: C) They can appear in answers that read fluently and hold together from start to finish.
D) They are a known limit of current frontier models, not a sign of a broken setup.
explanations: Brevity does not confer accuracy. A one-line answer can contain an invented figure just as easily as a long one, and offers fewer clues to catch it.
Web access changes where material comes from but does not remove the possibility of a misstatement, including a source being summarised incorrectly.
Correct. Fluency and internal coherence are not evidence of truth, which is exactly why colleagues who judge by readability tend to miss fabricated content.
Correct. Framing this as a known model limitation is a separate and important point: colleagues should not assume a setting was configured wrongly and stop checking.
No instruction eliminates the behaviour. Asking for certainty can suppress useful hedging while leaving confident errors in place.
